title: Kunnen, willen, moeten, mogen
summary: The four modal verbs and the word order rule that pushes the infinitive to the end

blocks.title: De vier modale werkwoorden
blocks.body: **kunnen** (can/be able), **willen** (want), **moeten** (must/have to), **mogen** (may/be allowed to) are Dutch's politeness engine — swap one for another and the whole tone of a sentence changes. All four are irregular in the singular.

blocks.title: Modaal + infinitief aan het einde
blocks.body: Dutch stacks two verbs like this: **the modal takes position 2 (V2), and the plain infinitive gets pushed all the way to the end of the clause.** *Ik wil een koffie bestellen.* (I want to order a coffee.) *Kun je me helpen?* (Can you help me?) *Je moet dit proeven!* (You must try this!)
blocks.callout: Never *ik wil bestellen een koffie* — the infinitive always waits at the end.

blocks.title: moeten vs mogen — obligation vs permission

pairs.left: Je moet stoppen. — you must stop
pairs.right: Je mag stoppen. — you're allowed to stop
pairs.note: moeten forces you, mogen gives you permission — the classic beginner mix-up. Confusing them can flip a sentence's meaning completely.

blocks.prompt: Which modal expresses polite permission, not obligation?
blocks.explain: *mogen* — 'may/is allowed to'. *moeten* is the one that forces you.

blocks.title: Build a modal sentence
blocks.prompt: Modal in position 2, infinitive at the end — assemble a sentence.
Type: 'Can you help me?' — use kunnen.
blocks.hint: Modal + je + me + helpen, infinitive at the end.
blocks.explain: *Kun je me helpen?* — inversion drops the -t: *kun je*, not *kunt je*.

blocks.prompt: Listen and type what you hear.
Write three sentences about yourself using kunnen, willen, and moeten — remember, the infinitive goes at the end!
